"Well, Jup," I said, "what's wrong now? How is your master?"

"To tell the truth, sir, he isn't as well as he ought to be."

"Unwell! I'm very sorry to hear that. What does he complain about?"

"That's just it! He doesn't complain of anything, but he's very sick all the same."

"Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn't you tell me at once? Is he stuck in bed?"

"No, he isn't! He won't stay anywhere. That's the trouble. I'm terribly worried about poor Master Will."

"Jupiter, I wish I could understand what you're telling me. You say your master is sick. Hasn't he explained what's wrong?"

"Now, sir, there's no need to get angry. Master Will says nothing is wrong at all. But why does he walk around like this, head down and shoulders up, looking white as a ghost? And he keeps ciphering all the time—"

"He keeps doing what, Jupiter?"

"Ciphering, with numbers on a slate—the strangest figures I've ever seen. I'm getting scared, I tell you. I have to watch his movements very closely. The other day he slipped away before sunrise and stayed out all blessed day. I'd cut a big stick ready to give him a good beating when he returned. But I'm such a fool I couldn't bring myself to do it—he looked so poorly."

"Eh? What? Oh, yes. Well, I think you'd better not be too hard on the poor fellow. Don't beat him, Jupiter; he couldn't stand it. But have you any idea what caused this illness, or rather, this change in his behaviour? Has anything upsetting happened since I last saw you?"

"No, sir, nothing bad has happened since then. I'm afraid it was before that—on the very day you visited."

"How? What do you mean?"

"I mean the bug, sir. That's it."

"The what?"

"The bug. I'm quite sure that gold bug bit Master Will somewhere around his head."

"What grounds do you have for thinking that, Jupiter?"

"Plenty of claws, sir, and a mouth too. I've never seen such a devilish bug. It kicked and bit at everything that came close. Master Will caught it first, but he had to drop it again mighty fast, I tell you. That must be when it bit him. I didn't like the look of its mouth myself, no indeed, so I wouldn't pick it up with my fingers. I caught it with a piece of paper I found."

"Basil, how remarkable! I must meet Dorian Gray."

Hallward rose from the seat and paced along the garden. After a while he returned. "Harry," he said, "Dorian Gray is merely an artistic inspiration to me. You might find nothing in him; I find everything. Nowhere is he more present in my paintings than where his likeness does not appear. As I told you, he suggests a new approach. I discover him in the bend of particular lines, in the beauty and delicacy of particular colours. That is the whole of it."

"Why, then, do you refuse to show his portrait?" Lord Henry asked.

"Because I have inadvertently expressed in it something of this strange worship I feel as an artist, something I have naturally never wished to mention to him. He has no knowledge of it, and never shall. The public might divine it, however, and I refuse to expose my soul to their superficial, inquisitive gaze. They shall never place my heart beneath a microscope. The picture contains too much of me, Harry—far too much!"

"Poets have fewer scruples than you. They appreciate the publishing value of passion. A broken heart these days can fill edition after edition."

"And I despise them for it," Hallward exclaimed. "An artist ought to make beautiful things without introducing anything of his personal life. In our age, people approach art as though it were intended for autobiography. We have forgotten beauty in the abstract. One day I shall teach the world what it means, and for that very reason the world must never look upon my portrait of Dorian Gray."

"I believe you're mistaken, Basil, but I shan't dispute it. Only the intellectually bewildered ever argue. Tell me, does Dorian Gray care very much for you?"

The painter thought for several moments. "He likes me," he replied at last. "I am sure of that. Naturally, I flatter him outrageously. There is an odd pleasure in telling him things I know I shall afterward regret. Generally he treats me charmingly; we sit together in the studio discussing a thousand subjects. Sometimes, though, he is terribly inconsiderate and appears positively to enjoy hurting me. At those times, Harry, I feel I have surrendered my entire soul to someone who regards it as a flower for his buttonhole, a little embellishment to gratify his vanity, an ornament to wear upon a summer afternoon."

You won't, eh? Oh, you magnificent simpleton!"

"It's wicked, isn't it, Oliver?" Charley Bates asked. "He'll end up scragged, won't he?"

"I don't understand that word," Oliver replied.

"Something like this, old chap," said Charley. Taking one end of his neckerchief, Master Bates held it upright, let his head fall sideways upon his shoulder, and forced a peculiar noise between his teeth. This spirited pantomime demonstrated that scragging meant precisely the same thing as hanging.

"That's the meaning," Charley said. "See him staring, Jack! I never knew such capital company as that boy. He'll be the death of me, I'm certain." After another hearty fit of laughter, Master Charley Bates returned to his pipe with watering eyes.

"Your upbringing's been all wrong," observed the Dodger, admiring his boots with great satisfaction now that Oliver had polished them. "But Fagin will turn you into something, unless you're the first boy he ever had who didn't pay. You'd best make a start now. You'll be in the business sooner than you imagine, and all you're doing is wasting time, Oliver."

Master Bates supported this counsel with several moral exhortations of his own. When these were spent, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins began an enthusiastic account of the many delights attending their way of life. Throughout, they offered Oliver various hints that his wisest course was to win Fagin's approval immediately, employing the methods by which they had won it themselves.

"And remember this, Nolly," said the Dodger, as the Jew could be heard unlocking the upper door, "if you don't nab fogels and tickers—"

"What's the use of talking like that?" Master Bates interrupted. "He hasn't a notion what you're saying."

"If you don't take pocket-handkerchiefs and watches," the Dodger continued, bringing his language within Oliver's understanding, "another fellow will. The fellows who lose them will suffer, and so will you, and nobody gains half a penny except whoever gets them. You've as much right to them as those fellows have."

"Certainly, certainly!" said the Jew, who had come in without Oliver noticing. "That's the whole matter in a nutshell, my dear; a nutshell. Trust the Dodger. Ha! ha! ha! He knows his profession's catechism."

The old man rubbed his hands joyfully while thus endorsing the Dodger's argument, chuckling in delight at his pupil's accomplishments.

The discussion went no further then. The Jew had brought Miss Betsy home with him, together with a gentleman Oliver had never met, whom the Dodger greeted as Tom Chitling. Having paused upon the stairs to exchange a few compliments with the lady, this gentleman now appeared.
